summary_plain: This ground-based investigation studies how hot flames transition into cool flames and how cool flame flammable regions relate to extinction limits. By combining data from space experiments with new simulations and ground setups, researchers examine parameters like oxygen concentration and pressure. This knowledge helps improve spacecraft fire safety by advancing our understanding of unusual, near-limit combustion behaviors.
summary_expert: The investigation conducted new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to study cool flame transitions and flammability limits. Using experimental conditions from FLEX flight data, researchers applied three numerical modeling schemes including spark-assisted flame propagation of n-heptane/air mixtures, one-dimensional freely-propagating DME flames, and simulated regimes at elevated pressure up to 20 atm using DME/air mixtures. Results demonstrated that the warm flame features a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in transitions between cool and hot flames, while the flammable region of warm and cool flames expands at elevated pressures due to increased low- and intermediate-temperature reactivity.

key_findings.text: The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames.
At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure.
Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications.
